sentences.text: Acamptonectes was a marine reptile with a dolphin-like body shape that allowed it to reach a length of 3 meters.
The genus name refers to adaptations that made the animal's trunk rigid, including tightly fitting skull bones, interlocking vertebrae, and strongly rounded ribs that increased resistance to bending.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is considered an adult due to extensive bone fusion within the occiput and a smooth humerus texture, and it possessed disc-shaped vertebrae that were deeply concave on both ends.
Its snout had a depth-to-length ratio of 0.044, which is one of the lowest among ophthalmosaurids.
While the color of Acamptonectes is unknown, some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark in life, supported by evidence of eumelanin pigments in early ichthyosaur skin fossils.
Acamptonectes is significant because it proves ophthalmosaurine ichthyosaurs survived the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary extinction event.
Ichthyosaurs like Acamptonectes were viviparous, giving birth to live young, and were likely unable to leave the water.
The genus Acamptonectes was established by Fischer et al. in 2012, with the type species being Acamptonectes densus.
The first and most complete specimen was discovered in 1958 in the Speeton Clay formation of North Yorkshire, England, where it was collected by students and a technician from Hull University.
Although the first specimen was found in 1958, the genus was not formally described until 2012.
A partial subadult skeleton was identified from Cremlingen, Germany, along with specimens from other English localities, including late Hauterivian rocks near Cremlingen in the Lower Saxony Basin.
The holotype was found in the D2D beds, while another specimen came from the slightly older D2C beds.
Ferdinand Broili named a specimen Ichthyosaurus brunsvicensis in 1909 but considered the assignment tentative.

Acamptonectes fed on soft, fleshy prey like fish and squid using slender, ridged teeth adapted for impaling, and researchers suggest it was likely a generalist predator despite having eyes adapted for depth diving.
The enlarged olfactory region in ichthyosaur brains indicates they possessed a sensitive sense of smell.
Researchers suggest the long neural spines of Acamptonectes may be bony extensions analogous to extraneural processes found in juvenile Stenopterygius.
A 2012 study classified Acamptonectes as a member of the family Ophthalmosauridae, and it belongs to the parent group Ophthalmosaurinae.
A 2012 phylogenetic analysis found Acamptonectes most closely related to Ophthalmosaurus natans.
Phylogenetic analysis by Fischer et al. indicates that the family Ophthalmosauridae experienced an early divergence into two very distinct subfamilies, Ophthalmosaurinae and Platypterygiinae.
Acamptonectes fossils date to the Hauterivian stage of the Early Cretaceous, living during the Early Cretaceous period from 132.6 to 125.77 million years ago.

The discovery of Acamptonectes provides evidence against a mass extinction of ichthyosaurs at the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary, as studies indicate a net extinction rate of zero for ophthalmosaurids at that time, suggesting they remained very diverse until their total extinction at the end of the Early Cretaceous.
